Command Structure
Organization
Formations
The basic administrative formation in the army was the company, about 150 men. Eight companies formed a regiment, and four companies made a battalion, whose strength was 500–600 men. This structure had remained the same since the reign of Charles XI. Under Gustav IV Adolf, the brigade was reintroduced, grouping 3–6 battalions after the French model. The cavalry switched from the Carolean structure to smaller units; the company became the smallest tactical unit, and the name, squadron, was transferred to this new tactical unit, with regiments reorganized to comprise five squadrons. The artillery was divided in 1794 into several new regiments, each with field and fortress units.
Logistics
Since the reign of Gustavus Adolphus, the army's peacetime logistics, consisting of provisioning, clothing, and pay, were overseen through cooperation between the Krigskollegium, local authorities, and regiments. In wartime, however, no permanent logistical structure existed; instead, ad hoc organizations under a General Commissioner for War (generalkrigskommissariat) oversaw supply, transport, and medical care through requisitioned civilian labor. This system proved relatively effective when conflicts allowed for preparation and enemy logistical capabilities were similarly underdeveloped.
